title: "Am I not your Lord?"
hookLine: the souls of Adam's children are asked, am I not your Lord, and say, yes (7:172)
last: ARINI — THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.

cards: A song heard for the first time that seems already known. A street never walked before that somehow says, I know this. Persian poets had a name for an older version of that feeling: the day of Alast.
They meant a moment before anyone was born, when every human soul heard a single question and gave a single answer.
They took it from one verse in surah seven, and Alast is simply the first word of that question in Arabic.

teach.b: Verse one-seventy-two says your Lord brought out from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify about themselves.
Then the question, in Pickthall's words: “Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify.” In Arabic: alastu bi-rabbikum? Qalu bala.
The verse gives the reason: so that no one can say on the Day of Resurrection, we didn't know about this.

Scholars call this al-mithaq, the covenant, from a root meaning to bind firmly, like a rope tied tight; the word appears in the verses just before. What exactly happened? Muslim scholars read it two main ways.
Some, citing a hadith in which Umar asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about this verse, take it as a real event: every soul drawn out and asked, before the world began.

Others read it as a picture of human nature itself, the fitrah: every person made with knowledge of their Lord built in, the testimony written into who they are. Both readings agree on the most striking part.
In this telling, faith isn't something foreign added later. It's remembering. Sufi poets took this up.

Rumi wrote of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, crying out to go home, and some readers hear in that the soul longing for the day it said yes. The Qur'an's own word for the answer is tiny: bala. Yes.

how: Muslims teach 7:172 as the primordial covenant (al-mithaq) and link it to the fitrah, the natural disposition toward God; Sufi poets, especially in Persian, call it the day of Alast.

o: a holy promise made by a pilgrim at Mecca
the Day when every soul is finally judged
the covenant: a firm pledge, sworn before birth

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the nature people are made with

s: the word Alast comes from the first word of the question
all Muslim scholars read 7:172 as a literal event

games.q: every soul hears the question: am I not your Lord? what do they answer in 7:172?
games.why: qalu bala, shahidna: they said, yes, we testify.

practice: Imagine, just for a moment, that before your first breath you were asked a question and you answered; you don't have to decide what you believe about it, just sit inside the picture.
Then, if it fits, let the word bala, yes, pass through your mind on one quiet out-breath, and if it doesn't, notice what in you wants to say yes to something larger.

wordCard.voice: Mithaq. The covenant: the firm pledge of 7:172, when the children of Adam were asked, am I not your Lord, and said, yes. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a covenant, a firm pledge, from w-th-q, to bind firmly.

carryVoice: Your line: we said yes. A familiar feeling can be a small remembering. Four hundred thirteen days now.
